messages.subject: area_of_areas and expansion
parts:
Hi Nick,


I’m interested in seeing if I can use BioGeoBEARS to address the following question: Which is associated with higher levels of cladogenesis, an increase in similar habitat (eg sea level retreat) or an addition of novel habitat? I’m brainstorming ways to do this, and one idea would require explicit expansion of a given area over time. I saw that there is an area_of_areas feature, but from what I could find (the “areas_allowed and dispersal_multipliers” post) that seems to be focused on extinction/range contraction. Could it be used for the opposite (eg maybe by setting the 'd' parameter to free?), or are the models not designed to handle that?


Note: I have done a successful basic run through with BioGeoBEARS and read most of the documentation, but my understanding of the inner workings may still be naïve.


Thanks,

Anne

parts:
On Thursday, October 11, 2018 at 3:43:51 AM UTC+13, anneth...@gmail.com wrote:

Hi Nick,


I’m interested in seeing if I can use BioGeoBEARS to address the following question: Which is associated with higher levels of cladogenesis, an increase in similar habitat (eg sea level retreat) or an addition of novel habitat? I’m brainstorming ways to do this, and one idea would require explicit expansion of a given area over time. I saw that there is an area_of_areas feature, but from what I could find (the “areas_allowed and dispersal_multipliers” post) that seems to be focused on extinction/range contraction. Could it be used for the opposite (eg maybe by setting the 'd' parameter to free?), or are the models not designed to handle that?


Note: I have done a successful basic run through with BioGeoBEARS and read most of the documentation, but my understanding of the inner workings may still be naïve.


Thanks,

Anne

Hi -- this is a complex question.  

Re: the "area of areas" feature -- this was coded up to be a modifier on the "e" process (the rate of range contraction aka rate of extirpation in an area).  One can easily imagine, for instance, that this rate would be higher in areas that are smaller.  However, the inference of the "e" parameter is so poor in most models, that I never seriously pursued trying to infer modifiers for "e".

Background on inference of "e" :

1. Poor inference of "e" was noted in Ree & Smith 2008 for the DEC model

2. It seems to be similarly poor in most other models -- the basic problems are 

2a. transitions like A->null and B->null are allowed in the model, but the "null range" is almost never observed in actual data.  As the null range is never observed, the inference "thinks" that the rate of going from A->null, B->null, etc., must be low, therefore "e" must be low (usually 0).  There are some exceptions, e.g. if you have many species occupying 2, 3, 4 etc. ranges, but this is fairly rare

2b. in a sense, the "e" process is competing with vicariance etc. as ways to "reduce range size", since the cladogenesis processes typically produce average ranges smaller than the parent range, it is hard to get signal for e


3. Inference of "e" probably works better in a model like BAYAREALIKE model (but not BAYAREALIKE+J), because vicariance etc are disallowed, so the only way to have sisters with ranges (A,B) requires both a "d" and "e" event.  However, the BAYAREALIKE model has its own issues -- e.g. it is usually the worst-fitting base model. 

4. Another option is to remove the null range from the state space, this is done in the "+*" models, e.g. DEC* (DECstar), discussed in Massana et al 2016 on bioRxiv:

Non-null Effects of the Null Range in Biogeographic Models - bioRxiv
https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2015/09/16/026914

...Massana et al. show in simulations that this dramatically improves inference of "e". However, the "+x" solution has its own peculiarities, namely

4a. "e" often goes to infinity on empirical datasets (specifically, empirical datasets where most tips live in single areas, which is common...read Massana et al for why)
4b. Arguably, if AB->B is an allowed transition, then A->null should be allowed also
4c. It seems like changing the state space is "changing the data", and statistical model comparison requires fitting different models to identical data


As suggested in Massana et al., the real solution to the "e" problem is probably using a full SSE model, where instead of having transitions like A->null, instead you have a rate of lineage extinction for a lineage with range A (this suggestion goes back to Fitzjohn).  The complexity here is that for computation speed reasons, SSE models have only been run on fairly small state spaces, e.g. a few dozen states as of 2018.  In biogeography models we often have hundreds or thousands of states in the state space.

Anyhow: getting back to your question,

* The simple/crude way to answer it would just be to do Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping for your clade, count the number of different events through time, and then see if you observe an increase between when an area was thought increase in size.  Repeat over a collection of dated phylogenies to account for dating uncertainty.

* The best way would be to use a full SSE model and explicitly propose a model (e.g. in diversitree) where the speciation rate varies as a function of the area size through time, and see if you get statistical support for that over a null model where the speciation rate is independent.  However, I expect this would require a large tree (to have a chance of getting signal) and perhaps an SSE implementation that can scale up to a sufficient number of states, depending on the size of your state space.

Cheers,
Nick
